from collections import defaultdict


def sum_of_distances(nums):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        groups[x].append(i)
    ans = [0] * len(nums)
    for idxs in groups.values():
        total = sum(idxs)
        prefix = 0
        for k, i in enumerate(idxs):
            left = i * k - prefix
            right = (total - prefix - i) - i * (len(idxs) - k - 1)
            ans[i] = left + right
            prefix += i
    return ans
why: The dict of index lists stores exactly n indices in total, so the nested loop over the groups and each sum(idxs) touch every index a constant number of times (O(n) time), and the groups plus the answer array take O(n) space.
All 2^n bitmasks are enumerated and each one scans n bits, giving O(n * 2^n) time, while only a few integer counters are kept (range is lazy), so space is O(1).

In the worst case (longest palindromic prefix of length 1) the loop runs n times and each iteration builds a slice of length i and its reverse at O(i) cost, for O(n^2) total, while the slices and the returned string are O(n) space.
Each recursive call divides the value n by 5, so there are O(log n) calls doing O(1) work each, and the recursion stack is O(log n) frames deep.
Sorting a copy costs O(n log n) and the two pointers then close in on each other in O(n), while sorted() allocates a new list of n elements, so space is O(n).

Although a while loop sits inside the for loop, left only moves forward, so each element is inserted and erased at most once with O(1) hash operations (O(n) time), and the window set can hold up to n distinct values (O(n) space).

The indices i and j only move left across the string, each substr copies one word once, and std::string += is amortised O(1) per character, so the nested whiles total O(n) time, and the result string (plus one temporary word) is O(n) space.
After an O(n log n) sort of a copy, each of the O(n^2) pairs (i, j) runs a lower_bound binary search costing O(log n), giving O(n^2 log n) time, and the sorted copy uses O(n) space.
Every cell of the (n+1) x (m+1) DP table is filled in O(1), so time is O(n * m), and the whole table is kept in memory, so space is O(n * m).
The loop always runs exactly 32 times regardless of the value of n and only two integers are stored, so both time and space are O(1).
For each d the inner loop runs n/d times and the harmonic sum n/1 + n/2 + ... + n/n is O(n log n), while the returned count vector has n + 1 entries, so space is O(n).

Java String += copies the whole accumulated string on every append, so with up to n kept characters the copies sum to O(n^2) time (the vowel lookup is in a constant 10-character string), and the result string is O(n) space.
One pass over the n elements with O(1) hash map lookups and updates gives O(n) time, and the map can hold up to n + 1 distinct prefix sums, so space is O(n).
Sorting the copied array dominates at O(n log n) while the two scans are O(n), and the copy plus the result list of up to n - 1 pairs take O(n) space.
Binary search halves the range [lo, hi) on every iteration, so it takes O(log n) time using only a few index variables, O(1) space.

All O(n^2) index pairs (i, j) are checked by a two-pointer palindrome test costing O(j - i), which for a string of identical characters sums to O(n^3), and only index variables are used, so space is O(1).
Two sequential linear passes give O(n) time, and the returned result array of length n counts as allocated space under these conventions, so space is O(n).
indexOf and lastIndexOf each scan the array in O(n) and are called for every one of the n elements, so time is O(n^2), while only a counter is kept, so space is O(1).

Row i has i + 1 entries computed in O(1) each, so with n = numRows the dependent loops do 1 + 2 + ... + n = O(n^2) work, and all rows are returned, O(n^2) space.

from typing import List


def level_sums(heap: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    # heap stores a complete binary tree level by level
    n = len(heap)
    sums = []
    start, width = 0, 1
    while start < n:
        end = min(start + width, n)
        total = 0
        for i in range(start, end):
            total += heap[i]
        sums.append(total)
        start = end
        width *= 2
    return sums
why: The level width doubles each round, so the inner loop visits each of the n elements exactly once across O(log n) levels (O(n) total), and the returned list holds one sum per level, O(log n).

Each of the O(n^2) (start, end) pairs first builds the slice s[start:end] of length up to n, so the worst case with no early break (e.g. an empty word set) is O(n^3), while the DP array and the one live slice use O(n) space.
For every prefix length i the code copies and sorts the prefix in O(i log i), which sums to O(n^2 log n), while the current sorted copy plus the n-element result list use O(n) space.
Trial division stops once d*d exceeds the shrinking n, so the worst case (n prime) runs about sqrt(n) iterations with only O(log n) extra divisions, and the factor list holds at most log2(n) entries.
The double loop fills n*m DP cells (n = len(a), m = len(b)) in O(1) each, but only two preallocated rows of length m+1 are kept and swapped, so space is O(m).

Building and comparing the two concatenations costs O(n + m) and dominates the O(log min(n, m)) Euclid loop on the lengths and the O(gcd) result slice, and the temporary concatenations take O(n + m) space.
Merge sort does O(n) merging and counting work on each of its O(log n) recursion levels, and it allocates one shared n-element buffer plus an O(log n) recursion stack, so O(n) space.
Each of the (n+1) x (m+1) cells (n = |word1|, m = |word2|) is filled once in O(1) and the full table is kept, so both time and space are O(n * m).
Each of the n elements performs one O(log n) lower_bound binary search over the tails array, and tails can grow to n entries.
Each recursive call halves the exponent n, so there are O(log n) calls doing O(1) work each, and the recursion stack is O(log n) frames deep.
The interval DP loops over chain length, start index and split point, each O(n), giving O(n^3) time, and it stores an n x n cost table, O(n^2) space.
Only a constant number of arithmetic and min/max operations on scalar arguments are performed, with no loops or allocations.

With the last element as pivot, a sorted or all-equal array peels off only one element per call, so partitioning costs n + (n-1) + ... = O(n^2) and the recursion is n frames deep, O(n) space (the array is sorted in place and returned without copying).

For each of the n items the inner loop sweeps capacities from m = capacity down to the item's weight (up to m+1 steps), giving O(n * m) time, while the single rolling array has m+1 entries, O(m) space.
Sorting the n intervals costs O(n log n) and the merge is one linear scan, while the merged list and the returned array hold up to n intervals, O(n) space.
Each value from 1 to n is computed in O(1) from the stored answer for i >> 1, and the returned array has n+1 entries.
Binary search on the answer over [0, x] halves the range every iteration, so it runs O(log n) times for n = x, using only a few scalar variables.
Each of the 2n-1 centres can expand O(n) steps (e.g. a string of one repeated letter), giving O(n^2) time, and the only allocation is the returned substring of length up to n.

On strictly ascending input every node walks the whole sorted prefix before being linked at its end, so the scans total 1 + 2 + ... + n = O(n^2), and the existing nodes are relinked in place with a single dummy node, O(1) space.
The loop always runs exactly 32 times no matter how large x and y are, and only scalars are used, so time and space are constant.
Copying and sorting the m potions costs O(m log m) and each of the n spells then does an O(log m) binary search, while the sorted copy (m) and the result array (n) need O(n + m) space.
All 2^n - 1 non-empty bitmasks are enumerated and each one scans all n bits, giving O(n * 2^n) time, with only scalar accumulators for O(1) space.
The first pass strips the O(log n) digits of n and leaves a digit sum of only O(log n) magnitude, so the later passes add just O(log log n) and the total is O(log n), using constant space.
Three separate linear passes over the n ratings give O(n) time, and the candies array has n entries, O(n) space.
Bubble sort of the copied slice does O(n^2) comparisons on reverse-ordered input (the early exit never fires), followed by an O(n) comparison pass, and the expected copy takes O(n) space.
For each d the inner loop runs n/d times, and n/1 + n/2 + ... + n/n is the harmonic sum O(n log n), while the returned slice has n+1 entries.
Every cell of the n x m grid is visited once with O(1) work, and the running minima are written back into the input grid, so no auxiliary memory is allocated.
Each call halves the search interval, so there are O(log n) calls, and because Go does not eliminate tail calls the recursion stack is O(log n) frames deep.
A single greedy pass over the n positions does O(1) work per index and keeps only three scalar variables.
The interval DP fills each of the roughly n^2/2 cells with i <= j once in O(1), and it allocates a full n x n table, O(n^2) space.
Dividing n by 5 on every iteration means the loop runs about log5(n) times, so O(log n) time with two scalar variables and no factorial ever computed.
Each of the n*m character pairs updates one table cell in O(1), and the zero-initialised (n+1) x (m+1) table is kept in full, so space is O(n * m).
Every element branches into a minus and a plus call, so the recursion tree has 2^(n+1) - 1 calls (O(2^n) time), but only one root-to-leaf path of n+1 frames is on the stack at once, O(n) space.

Kadane's rolling DP does O(1) work per element and keeps only the best sum ending at the current index and the overall best.
Binary search on the answer length takes O(log n) rounds, each checking every window of that length with an O(n) sliding sum, and only scalar variables are used.
Each of the n calls copies the slice s[1:] and builds rest + s[0], both O(n), for O(n^2) time, and every frame on the n-deep stack keeps its own slice alive, so the copies total O(n^2) space.
The three-way recursion looks exponential, but lru_cache computes each of the n + 1 states once with O(1) work, so time is O(n), and the cache plus the n-deep recursion use O(n) space.

from typing import List


def subsets(nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
    result = []
    path = []

    def backtrack(i: int) -> None:
        if i == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i])
        backtrack(i + 1)
        path.pop()
        backtrack(i + 1)

    backtrack(0)
    return result
why: The include/exclude recursion reaches 2^n leaves and copies a path of up to n elements at each, giving O(n * 2^n) time, and the returned list holds 2^n subsets with O(n * 2^n) total elements.

Each leaf copies its whole root-to-leaf path, and a tree made of a long spine ending in a bushy subtree has O(n) leaves at depth O(n), so the copies cost O(n^2) time and the returned paths hold O(n^2) values.
Each call removes one decimal digit, so there are O(log n) calls doing O(1) work and the recursion stack is O(log n) frames deep.
The node is deleted by copying its successor's value and unlinking the successor, a fixed number of pointer operations with no allocation.
Every node is visited once with O(1) work, and the recursion depth equals the tree height, which is n for a chain-shaped tree.
Swap-based backtracking generates all n! orderings and copies the n-element vector at each leaf, giving O(n * n!) time, and the result stores n! vectors of length n, O(n * n!) space.
There are O(n^2) memoised (i, j) intervals and each tries O(n) split points, giving O(n^3) time, while the n x n memo table dominates the O(n) recursion depth for O(n^2) space.
countFrom takes the vector by value, so each of the n + 1 calls copies all n elements (O(n^2) time) and every frame of the n-deep recursion holds its own copy (O(n^2) space).
The loop follows a single root-to-leaf path, which has n nodes in a degenerate chain-shaped BST, and keeps only one pointer.
Binary search over [0, x] halves the range each iteration, so it runs O(log n) times for n = x, using a constant number of variables.
The HashMap memo means each value from 3 to n is computed once with O(1) map operations, so time is O(n), and the memo plus the n-deep recursion take O(n) space.
BFS enqueues and dequeues every node exactly once, and the queue plus the returned per-level lists hold O(n) values.
Exponentiation by squaring halves the exponent n on every recursive call, so there are O(log n) calls with O(1) work each and the stack is O(log n) deep.
Each call consumes one node from one of the two lists, so there are at most n + m calls with O(1) work, and although no nodes are allocated the recursion is up to n + m frames deep.
move makes two recursive calls on n - 1 disks, T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + O(1) = O(2^n), while the recursion is only n frames deep.
Each of the n nodes scans its inorder range linearly to find the root, which sums to O(n^2) for a left-skewed tree, while the n new nodes and the up-to-n-deep recursion use O(n) space.
Each recursive call halves the search range, giving O(log n) calls with O(1) work and an O(log n)-deep recursion stack.
The memo table makes each of the n * m cells resolve once with O(1) work, and the n x m memo dominates the O(n + m) recursion depth.
The full inorder traversal visits all n nodes regardless of k and stores every value in an array, with recursion up to n deep for a skewed tree.
Floyd's fast pointer either reaches the end or catches the slow pointer within O(n) steps, and only two pointers are kept.
Without memoisation each call spawns two more, T(n) = T(n - 1) + T(n - 2) + O(1), which is exponential (O(2^n)), while the deepest chain of calls is only n frames.
Each call walks its sublist to find the middle in O(size) and splits it in half, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n), and the n new tree nodes dominate the O(log n) recursion depth.
The range is halved and the crossing sum scans the whole range, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n), and with no allocation the only extra space is the O(log n) recursion depth.

Each of the O(log n) levels of the segment tree merges n elements in total, giving O(n log n) time, and every node keeps its own sorted copy, so the returned tree stores n values per level, O(n log n) space.
Halving the range with O(1) work per call gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) = O(n) time, and the recursion is only O(log n) deep with nothing allocated.
Each node is rewired once with O(1) work, but the recursion descends n frames before unwinding, so space is O(n) even though no nodes are allocated.
The recursion follows one root-to-leaf path, which is n nodes long in a degenerate BST, so both the time and the recursion depth are O(n), plus a single new node.

Inserting at the head allocates exactly one node and sets two fields, independent of the list length.

Swapping the n(n-1)/2 pairs above the diagonal and then reversing each of the n rows touches every cell of the n x n matrix a constant number of times, giving O(n^2) time, and all swaps are in place, giving O(1) space.

from typing import List


def is_valid_sudoku(board: List[List[str]]) -> bool:
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            value = board[r][c]
            if value == '.':
                continue
            b = (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3
            if value in rows[r] or value in cols[c] or value in boxes[b]:
                return False
            rows[r].add(value)
            cols[c].add(value)
            boxes[b].add(value)
    return True
why: The board is always 9 x 9, so the double loop runs a fixed 81 times and the 27 sets hold at most 9 digits each, giving O(1) time and O(1) space.

from collections import deque
from typing import List


def find_order(num_courses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
    graph = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indegree = [0] * num_courses
    for course, pre in prerequisites:
        graph[pre].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for nxt in graph[node]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)
    return order if len(order) == num_courses else []
why: With V = num_courses and E = len(prerequisites), building the adjacency list and indegrees is O(V + E) and Kahn's algorithm dequeues each course once and decrements along each edge once, so time is O(V + E), while the adjacency list, indegree array, queue and returned order take O(V + E) space.
Each index is pushed onto and popped from the monotonic stack at most once, so the nested while loop is amortised O(n) in total, and the answer vector plus the stack use O(n) space.

With n total nodes spread over k lists, scanning the k heads costs O(k) and every node is pushed and popped once on a heap that never holds more than k nodes (O(log k) each), giving O(k + n log k) time, and the result relinks the existing nodes, so only the O(k) heap is extra space.

For two n x n matrices the i, k and j loops each run n times in the worst case of a dense matrix (the zero skip only helps sparse input), giving O(n^3) time, and the returned n x n product matrix takes O(n^2) space.

Each open cell gets its distance set before it is enqueued, so each of the n * m cells is dequeued at most once with 4 neighbour checks, giving O(n * m) time, and the n x m distance table plus the queue take O(n * m) space.

With 8-directional moves on the grid the minimum number of steps is the Chebyshev distance max(|dx|, |dy|), computed with a fixed number of arithmetic operations and no data structures, so time and space are O(1).

Every value is pushed onto inbox once, moved to outbox at most once and popped at most once, so the transfer loop is amortised O(1) per operation and O(n) over the n operations, and the two stacks plus the returned list hold O(n) values.

Despite three nested loops, the visited array ensures each of the n cities is popped once and each pop scans one row of the n x n adjacency matrix, so time is O(n^2), while visited and the explicit stack use O(n) space.

The loop runs 2n times over the circular array but each index is pushed once and popped at most once from the monotonic stack, so the work is amortised O(n), and the result array plus the stack use O(n) space.
Each of the n * m cells is appended exactly once as the four boundaries shrink, giving O(n * m) time, and the returned list holds all n * m values, giving O(n * m) space.

Counting is O(n) with O(1) hash operations, then up to n distinct keys pass through a min-heap capped at k + 1 entries at O(log k) each, giving O(n log k) time, and the frequency map can hold n distinct keys, giving O(n) space.
The n x m matrix is treated as one sorted array of n * m values and binary search halves the index range each step, giving O(log(n * m)) time with a few index variables, so O(1) space.

Each vertex is coloured and enqueued once and each adjacency-list entry is examined once when its vertex is dequeued, so BFS colouring is O(V + E) time, while the colour array and the queue use O(V) space.
A single pass over the n characters with O(1) push/pop per character is O(n) time, and a string of only opening brackets fills the stack with n entries, giving O(n) space.
Every one of the n * m entries is copied once into a newly allocated m x n matrix that is returned, so both time and space are O(n * m).

Each fresh orange is marked rotten before it is enqueued, so each of the n * m cells enters the queue at most once and is processed with 4 neighbour checks (read through a head index rather than shift), giving O(n * m) time, and the queue array can hold n * m entries, giving O(n * m) space.
The centre of a star graph appears in every edge, so comparing the endpoints of only the first two edges answers in O(1) time and O(1) space regardless of V + E.

On the n x n adjacency matrix of a complete graph every pair i < j is adjacent, so the innermost loop runs for all triples i < j < k (about n^3 / 6 iterations), giving O(n^3) time, and only a counter is kept, giving O(1) space.
For each of the n rows a binary search over the m sorted columns finds the first 1 in O(log m) steps, giving O(n log m) time, and only scalar variables are used, giving O(1) space.

With n the value of label, the doubling loop finds its depth in O(log n) steps and the second loop climbs one level per iteration, giving O(log n) time, and the returned path holds one label per level, giving O(log n) space.

Starting at the top-right corner, each step discards either a column or a row of the row- and column-sorted n x m matrix, so at most n + m steps are taken (O(n + m) time) using only two indices (O(1) space).
Two full passes over the n x m matrix give O(n * m) time, and the only extra memory is one boolean per row and one per column, giving O(n + m) space.

Sorting the n meetings by start is O(n log n) and each meeting performs at most one heap pop and one push at O(log n) each, giving O(n log n) time, and the min-heap of end times can grow to n entries, giving O(n) space.

With V = n and E = len(edges), building the adjacency list touches each edge twice and the visited-guarded DFS pushes each vertex once and scans each adjacency entry once, so time is O(V + E), and the adjacency list (2E entries) plus visited and the stack take O(V + E) space.
Only the two diagonals of the n x n matrix are read, at most two cells per loop iteration, so time is O(n) rather than O(n^2), and only a running total is kept, giving O(1) space.
Heapify is O(n) and each of the n - 1 extractions performs an iterative sift-down of O(log n) steps, giving O(n log n) time, and the array is sorted in place without recursion, giving O(1) space.

The exponent n (an integer value) is halved every iteration, so the loop runs O(log n) times and each 2 x 2 matrix product is constant work despite its nested loops, giving O(log n) time, and only fixed 2 x 2 arrays are used, giving O(1) space.

The dependent nested loop swaps each of the n(n-1)/2 pairs above the diagonal of the n x n matrix once, giving O(n^2) time, and unlike a transpose into a new matrix the swaps happen in place with one temporary, giving O(1) space.

With n the value of the integer parameter, the four boundary loops write each of the n^2 cells exactly once, giving O(n^2) time, and the returned n x n matrix plus the column-size array allocate O(n^2) memory.

Every dfs call either returns at once or marks a new land cell (which then makes 4 calls), so across all outer-loop starts the total work is O(n * m), and a snake-shaped island can make the recursion n * m frames deep, giving O(n * m) space.
When all distances are finite the k, i and j loops each run n times over the n x n distance matrix, giving O(n^3) time, and the matrix is relaxed in place, giving O(1) auxiliary space.
